topics.title: Design Coffee Vending Machine
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a coffee vending machine that serves espresso, cappuccino, latte and so on. Each drink consumes ingredients (water, milk, beans, sugar). The machine takes payment, checks inventory, brews, returns change and reports low stock. It tests **State** (machine modes), **Factory** (beverages from recipes) and inventory consistency.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Show the menu with prices. Only drinks with enough ingredients are selectable.
- Accept coins, notes or card. Return change or refund on cancel or failure.
- Deduct ingredients and dispense. A technician can refill and go into maintenance mode.
- Alert when an ingredient drops below a threshold.

**Non-functional**
- One transaction at a time; button presses while dispensing are rejected cleanly.
- Never keep money without dispensing: every failure path ends in a dispense or a refund.
- New drinks, recipes and payment methods plug in without touching the core flow.
- Recovers to a safe state after a power cut mid-transaction.

## Learn through a concrete example

You select a ₹30 coffee and insert ₹50. The machine needs water, beans, a cup and enough change. Taking payment is not the same as successfully dispensing a drink. Start with one machine and a small menu; make physical outcomes explicit before adding payment apps or remote monitoring.

The **recipe** describes ingredient quantities, **inventory** records available ingredients, and a **vend session** owns one customer's interaction. A state machine answers which actions are allowed at each stage: inserting money during maintenance must not accidentally start brewing.

## See preparation and a partial outcome

![Reserve ingredients and change before committing the physical action.](lessons/lld-11-flow.svg)

*Reserve ingredients and change before committing the physical action.*

![Physical evidence determines whether retry or refund is appropriate.](lessons/lld-11-failure.svg)

*Physical evidence determines whether retry or refund is appropriate.*

### Build and calculate

A recipe requiring 10 g beans and 150 ml water allows `min(beans/10, water/150, cups)` servings. With 95 g beans, 1,000 ml water and 20 cups, water limits capacity to six drinks. Inventory checks must reserve the whole recipe together; separately decrementing beans and then discovering no cup leaves inconsistent stock.

```text
VendSession: IDLE -> SELECTED -> FUNDED -> DISPENSING -> COMPLETE
Failures: SELECTED/FUNDED -> CANCELLED
          DISPENSING -> DELIVERY_UNCERTAIN -> RECONCILIATION
```

## Design details and alternatives

### Key abstractions

| Type | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `VendingMachine` | Context and facade; holds the current `MachineState` |
| `MachineState` | `Idle`, `Selecting`, `PaymentPending`, `Dispensing`, `Maintenance` |
| `Beverage` / `Recipe` | name, price, `Map<Ingredient, Integer>` quantities |
| `BeverageFactory` | `create(type)` builds a beverage from the recipe registry |
| `Inventory` | `hasEnough(recipe)`, `deduct(recipe)` (atomic), `refill` |
| `PaymentHandler` | Strategy: `CoinPayment`, `CardPayment`; change calculation |
| `InventoryObserver` | Low-stock alert |

```java
class Inventory {
    private final Map<Ingredient, Integer> stock = new EnumMap<>(Ingredient.class);
    synchronized boolean tryDeduct(Recipe r) {
        if (!r.needs().entrySet().stream().allMatch(e -> stock.get(e.getKey()) >= e.getValue())) return false;
        r.needs().forEach((ing, q) -> stock.merge(ing, -q, Integer::sum));
        return true;
    }
}
```

### Design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Recipes as data.** Don't make `Cappuccino extends Coffee` with hard-coded quantities. A recipe registry (loaded from config) plus a Factory means a new drink is a config entry. Use a Decorator only for user add-ons (extra shot, extra sugar).

**2. Check and deduct atomically.** "Check, then deduct" as two calls races if two dispense paths exist. A single `tryDeduct` under a lock is all-or-nothing.

**3. When to deduct versus when to charge.** Order: confirm availability, collect payment, reserve and deduct ingredients, dispense. If dispensing fails, refund and restore ingredients. Never take money for a drink you can't make.

**4. State pattern.** In `Maintenance`, selections are rejected. In `Dispensing`, cancel is rejected. Each state handles only its legal events.

**5. Menu availability is derived.** Recompute which drinks are selectable from inventory after every deduct or refill, and push that to the display (Observer).

### Ownership, boundaries and invariants

**Central design question:** Inventory reservation, money acceptance and physical dispensing are separate observable steps.

Machine owns SlotInventory and a VendSession. Product describes a SKU; Recipe or Selection maps it to ingredients when appropriate. PaymentAcceptor tracks tender; ChangePolicy selects available denominations; DispenserPort reports success or jam. RefundJournal records incomplete recovery.

**Correctness rule:** Never decrement sellable stock twice for one vend request. Do not claim successful delivery before the hardware confirms it. Accepted money must end in purchase, change, refund or an explicit recoverable balance.

```text
slot(id,sku,available,reserved); vend(id,sku,price_minor,tender_minor,state); cash(denomination,count)
```

### State machine and command contracts

```text
IDLE -> SELECTED -> FUNDED -> DISPENSING -> COMPLETE; JAMMED -> REFUND_PENDING -> REVIEW
```

### End-to-end execution trace

Select a product; validate stock and price; reserve stock; accept sufficient tender; verify change availability; journal the vend; dispense; on confirmation consume stock and return change; on jam reverse the reservation and initiate refund.

### Concurrency and recovery walkthrough

Two sessions select the last unit while an operator restocks. One inventory owner serializes reserve/commit/release; restocking must not overwrite reserved counts. Network payment callbacks use the vend operation ID.



### Policy choices and extension seams

State is helpful for selection/payment/dispense transitions. Different products can use Strategy for preparation. Do not let product factories control cash or mutate global inventory.

### Edge cases that change the design

Enough total money does not imply the machine can make change. Power loss after dispensing needs journal reconciliation. A refund actuator can fail too, so expose an operator-review state instead of looping forever.

### Verification and a practical lab

**Topic-specific cases:** Last-item race; exact change; impossible change; jam; duplicate confirmation; refund failure; restart during dispense.

**Lab:** Inject a jam after payment is accepted but before stock consumption. Recover the stock reservation and record the customer liability.

### Further reading

- [Java 21 concurrency contracts](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html) — synchronization and executor semantics.
- [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) — database guarantees differ from process locks.

## Work through the important decisions

Coin selection is a bounded change problem: available denominations and counts matter. A ₹20 difference does not prove a ₹20 coin is present. Reserve a feasible change plan before consuming money, or show an exact-change policy before purchase.

Once hot water has entered a cup, cancelling cannot restore the original ingredients. Record consumed quantities and waste; do not “roll back” physical brewing by incrementing every ingredient counter. Maintenance mode should block new sessions and reconcile cash/stock under an operator identity.

## Practise, then check your reasoning

1. **Does a new drink require another machine state?** Usually no. A new recipe changes data; new physical behaviour may need a new dispenser strategy.
2. **Can a failed sensor mean zero delivery?** Not necessarily. Distinguish known none from unknown.
3. **Exercise:** start with enough beans for two drinks but one cup. Race two purchases; only one may reserve a complete recipe. Then fail after brewing and verify consumed stock stays consumed.

topics.title: Google Search
topics.concepts: Crawling, indexing, inverted index, ranking, distributed search
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design web search like Google at a high level: crawl billions of pages, build an index, and answer keyword queries in ~100–200 ms with relevant ranked results. The building blocks are **crawling**, **inverted indexes**, **distributed search (scatter-gather)** and **ranking**.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Crawl the web politely, re-crawling pages according to how often they change.
- Index text, titles, links. Answer free-text queries with ranked results and snippets.
- Spelling correction and autocomplete (bonus).

**Non-functional**
- Query latency p99 ~200 ms. Huge read QPS (~100k/s). Freshness from minutes (news) to weeks.

**Scale:** 50B pages × ~100 KB ≈ 5 PB raw. A compressed index is still hundreds of TB, so it must be **sharded** across thousands of machines.

## Learn through a concrete example

Search for “Java lock” across a billion pages. Scanning every page on every request is too slow. Instead, an **inverted index** maps terms to documents containing them. Crawling discovers pages, indexing prepares searchable data, and ranking selects useful results. These are separate stages with different freshness and resource limits.

Begin with a thousand local documents and a deterministic tokenizer. Make search return document IDs and matched evidence before introducing web-scale crawling or machine-learned ranking.

## See the offline and online paths

![Query serving reads a published index generation rather than crawling on demand.](lessons/hld-11-flow.svg)

*Query serving reads a published index generation rather than crawling on demand.*

![Versioned publication avoids exposing half-built posting lists.](lessons/hld-11-failure.svg)

*Versioned publication avoids exposing half-built posting lists.*

### Calculate and trace

For one billion documents with an assumed 500 distinct indexed terms each, there are roughly 500 billion term-document associations before compression. This is not the same as raw page bytes. Posting-list compression, document IDs and sharding determine actual index size.

For query `java lock`, retrieve each term's postings and intersect or combine them under the query policy. Rank candidates using signals such as term relevance and document quality. A snippet should come from the matching document version, not an unrelated cached revision.

## Design details and alternatives

### Architecture

**Crawl:** a **URL frontier** (prioritised queues per host, for politeness and priority) feeds distributed **crawler** workers. They fetch (respecting robots.txt), deduplicate content (simhash), extract links back into the frontier, and store pages in a doc store.

**Index:** batch plus incremental pipelines tokenise and normalise text and build an **inverted index**: `term → posting list [(docId, positions, tf)]`, sorted by docId and compressed (delta plus varint). Also compute static signals: PageRank, spam score, freshness.

**Serve:** the index is **document-partitioned** into shards, each replicated. A query goes to a root aggregator, which scatters to every shard. Each shard returns its local top-k by a cheap score. The aggregator merges, then a re-ranker (ML) refines the top few hundred, and snippets come from a doc server.

### Key design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Document vs. term partitioning.** *Document-partitioned:* every shard holds the full index for a subset of docs, so a query hits all shards (fan-out). It's simple, load-balanced and tolerant: a missing shard just means slightly fewer results. *Term-partitioned:* a query only touches the shards for its terms, but multi-term intersections cross the network and hot terms create hotspots. Real engines use document partitioning.

**2. Tail latency with fan-out.** With 1,000 shards, a p99 query sees the p99.9 of shards. Mitigations: replicas plus **hedged requests**, early termination (tiered indexes with the best docs first), and partial results under a deadline.

**3. Ranking layers.** Lexical relevance (BM25), query-independent quality (PageRank), freshness, and learned ranking on the candidate set. Cheap-to-expensive cascades keep latency bounded.

**4. Freshness.** A small, fast **real-time index** for recent and news pages, merged with the large batch index at query time.

**5. Caching.** Query result caches catch the head (a large share of traffic is repeated queries). Posting-list caches handle hot terms.

### Scope, guarantees and sizing assumptions

**Correctness requirement:** A searchable document revision is associated with an index generation and canonical source identity.

Assume 1 billion documents x 20 KB extracted text: 20 TB text before postings and replicas. At 10 million queries/day: about 116/s average, with explicit peak/skew headroom. Inverted-index size depends on term distribution, positions and compression.

### API contracts and data ownership

```text
GET /search?q=...&cursor=...; crawler enqueue URL; document indexing update with revision
```

```text
Logical records (outline, not complete DDL):
document(id,url,canonical_url,revision,language); posting(term,doc_id,frequency,positions); crawl(url,next_fetch,etag)

Primary access/partitioning boundary:
term partitions or document shards for index; URL/document_id for crawl frontier and canonicalization
```

### Build the architecture in stages

**Stage 3 — Partition and isolate.** Partition around term partitions or document shards for index; URL/document_id for crawl frontier and canonicalization. Track ownership with a routing epoch or a database-native partition mechanism. Move virtual buckets or copy/backfill data with a verified cutover, rather than changing a modulo divisor and assuming records move themselves. Isolate bulk/background workloads from the latency-sensitive path and test the busiest tenant independently.

### Trace the critical request

Maintain a polite deduplicated frontier; fetch allowed pages; canonicalize and extract text; tokenize/normalize; build posting segments; merge and publish a consistent index generation; query fans out to index shards, merges top candidates and returns snippets.

### Deep dive: the decision that changes this system

An inverted index maps terms to documents; positional postings support phrase queries. BM25-like lexical ranking provides a strong baseline before semantic reranking. Search is not a full table scan with wildcard LIKE. Freshness updates and deletions must reach all relevant replicas.

### Failure and race-condition walkthrough

A shard is slow or missing. Return clearly degraded results under a deadline rather than waiting forever, and record coverage so ranking evaluation can distinguish partial results. Index-generation mismatch can produce duplicates or stale snippets.

### Security, tenancy and lifecycle

### Trade-offs and a starting recommendation

Document sharding scatters queries but localizes document updates; term sharding complicates multi-term joins. Web-scale crawling needs robots policy, rate limits and fetch isolation because URLs are untrusted network destinations.

### SLOs, failure drills and lab

Query p99, result relevance on labelled queries, index freshness, crawl error rate, shard coverage and indexing backlog.

**Test matrix:** Phrase query, typo/empty query, crawler redirect loop, duplicate canonical URLs, deleted pages, shard deadline and index generation rollover.

### Follow-up questions with answers

**What cannot be eventually consistent here?** The operation establishing this guarantee: A searchable document revision is associated with an index generation and canonical source identity.

**What is the first scaling pressure to test?** Use the actual workload: Assume 1 billion documents x 20 KB extracted text: 20 TB text before postings and replicas. At 10 million queries/day: about 116/s average, with explicit peak/skew headroom. Inverted-index size depends on term distribution, positions and compression.

**Which failure would invalidate the naive design?** A shard is slow or missing. Return clearly degraded results under a deadline rather than waiting forever, and record coverage so ranking evaluation can distinguish partial results. Index-generation mismatch can produce duplicates or stale snippets.

**Why not introduce every distributed component immediately?** Document sharding scatters queries but localizes document updates; term sharding complicates multi-term joins. Web-scale crawling needs robots policy, rate limits and fetch isolation because URLs are untrusted network destinations.

**How would you demonstrate the design works?** Phrase query, typo/empty query, crawler redirect loop, duplicate canonical URLs, deleted pages, shard deadline and index generation rollover. Keep the expected invariant and recovery outcome visible in the results.

### Further reading

- [PostgreSQL isolation and anomalies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html).
- [Apache Kafka delivery and transaction design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/).
- [Redis rate-limiter design](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/rate-limiter/) for atomic shared-state examples.

## Work through freshness and abuse

Different pages change at different rates. Recrawl scheduling allocates budget using observed changes, importance and site limits. Canonicalization avoids indexing trivial URL variants repeatedly, but aggressive rules can merge genuinely different pages. Crawler network access must resist private-address fetching and resource exhaustion.

Partitioning by document keeps complete document metadata local but queries fan out. Partitioning by term changes query and update costs. Explain the selected access pattern before choosing a partition key. Spam, duplicate pages and deleted content need index-lifecycle handling, not only a ranking adjustment.

## Practise, then check your reasoning

1. **Does a crawler make search fast?** No. The prepared index does; crawling supplies input.
2. **Is top-10 from each shard automatically global top-10?** Only under compatible scoring and sufficient local candidates; distributed ranking needs an explicit merge contract.
3. **Exercise:** build term postings for ten documents, delete one and publish a new generation. Show how queries avoid mixed versions and how a failed rebuild preserves the previous usable index.

topics.title: Production RAG
topics.concepts: Chunking, metadata, hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Take RAG from demo to production: the techniques that move answer quality from "sometimes right" to dependable. That means smarter chunking with metadata, hybrid search, re-ranking, query rewriting and expansion, context compression, freshness and access control, and evaluation-driven tuning, plus how Spring AI's modular RAG components map onto them.

## Requirements

- Advanced chunking (structure-aware, parent-child, contextual headers).
- Hybrid lexical + semantic retrieval and rank fusion.
- Re-ranking with cross-encoders or LLM rankers.
- Query transformation: rewriting, multi-query, HyDE, conversational compression.
- Operational concerns: incremental ingestion, dedup, ACLs, evals and monitoring.

## Learn through a concrete example

A demonstration answers correctly from one PDF. Production adds thousands of documents, changing permissions, conflicting revisions and questions whose answers are absent. Production RAG makes evidence lifecycle and measurable failure behaviour part of the design rather than treating retrieval as a single library call.

**Recall@k** measures whether relevant evidence appears among retrieved candidates. A **reranker** reorders candidates with a more expensive relevance judgement. **Groundedness** evaluates whether the answer is supported by selected evidence. Improve the failing stage instead of blindly increasing every limit.

## See retrieval stages and a permission change

![Each stage leaves evidence for diagnosis and versioned evaluation.](lessons/ai-11-flow.svg)

*Each stage leaves evidence for diagnosis and versioned evaluation.*

![Evidence lifecycle extends beyond the primary document store.](lessons/ai-11-failure.svg)

*Evidence lifecycle extends beyond the primary document store.*

### Trace and calculate quality

On 100 answerable questions, relevant evidence may appear for 85. If 75 of those produce supported answers, retrieval recall is 85% while supported end-to-end success is 75% on that set. The conditional generation success is 75/85, about 88.2%. These diagnose different problems; one “accuracy” number hides them.

Reserve a separate unanswerable set. A system that confidently answers every question can score well on answer-present cases while failing dangerously when evidence is missing. Evaluate abstention precision/recall and critical security failures separately.

## Design details and alternatives

### Key concepts and learning objective

**Question to answer:** What turns a successful RAG demo into a dependable multi-tenant documentation product?

Production RAG is a lifecycle of ingestion, revisioning, retrieval, authorization, evaluation and operations. Hybrid search retrieves lexical and semantic candidates; reranking orders a small candidate set; context assembly removes duplicates and respects token budget.

### Architecture and contracts

```text
Source connector -> revision/ACL capture -> parse/chunk/embed -> staged index -> retrieval -> authorization -> rerank -> citation generation -> support verification

Application contracts (design outline):
IngestRun(sourceRevision,chunkerVersion,indexVersion,status); AnswerTrace(queryId,evidenceIds,promptVersion,modelVersion)
```

Use a simple QuestionAnswerAdvisor path as a baseline, then application-owned retrieval/reranking when policy requires it. Do not copy unversioned advisor constructors into a pinned build.

### Worked reasoning and capacity example

Assume 100 queries/s x 8 retrieved chunks x 600 tokens = 480,000 evidence tokens/s before history and output. Reranking all corpus chunks is impossible; first-stage retrieval must bound the candidate pool.

### Java and Spring AI implementation outline

```java
record RetrievalTrace(String queryId, String indexVersion,
    java.util.List<String> evidenceIds, String promptVersion) {}
// Log identities and counts, not raw private passages by default.
```

### Design decisions and alternatives

Evaluate retrieval failures before adding a larger model. Track data freshness and ACL updates as first-class work. Cache keys include tenant, permitted corpus version, prompt/model version and query normalization.

### Failure scenario and safe recovery

A shared semantic answer cache serves a correct answer to a user lacking access to the supporting documents. Partition caches by authorization domain and verify access on hits; similarity alone is not a safe cache key.

### Security, privacy and provenance

A more complex pipeline can be harder to debug and less reliable. Keep a measurable baseline and change one retrieval/generation component at a time.

### Hands-on lab and evaluation

**Build:** Replay a golden dataset against two chunkers and a hybrid pipeline. Add a document deletion, permission revocation, embedding outage and a cold-index rollback scenario.

**Measure:** Supported-answer rate, retrieval recall, citation correctness, abstention, p99 latency, indexing freshness and unauthorized evidence exposure. Slice metrics by tenant, language and document type.

### Further reading

- [Spring AI 1.1 ChatClient and request APIs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/chatclient.html).
- [Spring AI tool-execution boundary](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/tools.html).
- [MCP specification, versioned protocol concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18).
- [Original RAG research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) and [Transformer research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) for background rather than framework instructions.

## Work through release changes

Change one variable at a time: chunking, embedding model, hybrid weights, reranker or prompt. Version the corpus and expected evidence, then compare by topic, document age, language and answerability. A larger k increases latency/context and may add contradictory evidence; it is not an automatic quality improvement.

Cache keys need tenant, permission/freshness scope and relevant corpus/prompt/model versions. Similar questions are not sufficient grounds for sharing answers across users. Preserve source spans in traces so support review can inspect a claim without rerunning today's changed index.

## Practise, then check your reasoning

1. **Should generation be blamed when the source was never retrieved?** First diagnose retrieval; the generator cannot reliably cite missing evidence.
2. **Is a retrieval score a confidence score for the final answer?** No.
3. **Exercise:** create answer-present, absent, conflicting-version and revoked-source cases. Record retrieval candidates, packed evidence and final claims. Explain each failure at the responsible stage and compare one improvement against the same versioned suite.
